doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: Writing 'Cry': key, tenor harmonics and Dave Whitford
summary: She explains choosing A flat for the low B flat and altissimo notes on tenor, and the bass player Dave Whitford.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone

blocks.x: rewarding and interesting. And for me that has to be something creative because I think that’s where I want to go every day. What can I do that’s sort of an expression of something or a connection with something rather than maybe being a doctor wouldn’t be – who knows? It feels like it wouldn’t have been as rewarding for me. But it is a little different in that sense.

I want to ask you about at least one of your compositions that appears on your website, it’s called “Cry.” And it opens with, you know rubato. And I had two questions about it. First of all I think it’s in A flat. And I wondered if you picked that because it allows – because on your tenor you would be in a key that allows for harmonics. It’s helpful to be in that key to play those harmonics you were doing.

Yes. I think that’s in there. It’s also the low B flat as the bottom note and I love that note. And also, just as I was coming up with the first section of the melody, and the high F on tenor is a really nice note, and then it goes up to altissimo B flat. And that just felt quite – it’s quite a raw note, quite gritty, and it seemed to fit the atmosphere of that particular piece which is just really supposed to be very emotional, very raw and not sweet let’s say. So I think that’s why, yeah. And I wrote that, often I write at the piano, especially if it’s got harmony. But that piece of music is just that sort of A flat pedal, which of course isn’t the greatest for bass because it’s not an open string. But sometimes you have to ignore that. And also it’s Dave Whitford on bass and he’s just incredible so he’s happy to
Hell of a player. Yeah so it’s more about the high notes, that top B flat. But I think that might be such a satisfying note because of the harmonic structure of the saxophone.
